title: Technical deep dive: multi-region routing & failover - Northbridge
summary: SE-led technical deep dive on multi-region routing and failover design for Redwood inference platform. Discussed policy routing, regional capacity, DR playbooks, KV cache replication/consistency, batching/throughput tradeoffs, quantization impact on failover, VPC/on-prem considerations, and a phased test plan. Next steps agreed: Redwood to run a failover benchmark with Northbridge profile, share DR playbook draft and security/KMS checklist, and provide Dedicated/Private pricing and sizing options.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-08 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Recording: Yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Redwood SRE); Rachel Park (Northbridge), Dinesh Patel (Northbridge), Alicia Gomez (Northbridge Security)

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, uh quick check, does everyone see the slide deck i just dropped in the chat?
[00:00:12] Rachel Park: yep got it, thanks Maya. we're excited — we've been pulling together the reliability reqs for our inference layer.
[00:00:20] Maya Chen: awesome. the goal for today: deep dive on multi-region routing and failover — policy routing, regional capacity considerations, and a DR playbook you can run in a live incident. luis will lead the runtime/kv cache stuff.
[00:00:34] Luis Ortega: hi all, ill jump in on runtime impacts: batching, kv cache, quantization during failover, and what to expect latency/throughput-wise when we move traffic cross-region.
[00:00:45] Dinesh Patel: to set context, we operate in NA and EU, APAC is low volume. current SLOs: p95 < 300ms for short completions, p99 < 700ms. need RTO targets for inference < 5m for region outage and RPO for stateful caches close to zero if possible.
[00:01:05] Samir Rao: quick clarifying q — when you say 'stateful cache' you mean the KV cache for ongoing chat sessions? are you persisting to a central store or local node cache?
[00:01:15] Rachel Park: we currently keep session state in regional Redis clusters with async cross-region replication, it's eventual. for some financial workflows we need stronger consistency.
[00:01:29] Luis Ortega: ok that's typical. tradeoff: strict cross-region sync increases write latencies; for inference we often rely on prefix/KV cache to warm the model and skip re-computation. during failover you either accept cache miss cold-starts or replicate state synchronously which adds cost and latency.
[00:01:50] Alicia Gomez: security side — any cross-region replication has to meet our data residency and encryption in transit-at-rest rules; we use customer-managed keys in KMS. how does that work in Redwood Private?
[00:02:02] Samir Rao: in Private/VPC deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; keys stay in your cloud region. for hosted we support bring-your-own-key with region-limited key stores, but if you need full on-prem KMS we can do Private deploy.
[00:02:15] Maya Chen: great. luis, can you talk about routing policies — latency vs cost vs failover thresholds?
[00:02:22] Luis Ortega: yes. we use policy routing rules: primary region routing by latency and tier; fallback policies include region fallback (same model in next region), model variant fallback (quantized or lower-precision model for capacity), and tier fallback (move from Dedicated to Hosted for best-effort). triggers are health-check failures, elevated error rates, or sustained queuing > threshold.
[00:02:45] Luis Ortega: for health checks we recommend a combination: lightweight L7 check for quick detection (< 10s), synthetic inference probes that measure tail latency and accuracy correlation every 30s, and queue-depth/CPU/GPU util metrics with short windows.
[00:03:00] Dinesh Patel: what's the detection -> cutover timeline you typically see? we need to hit RTO < 5m.
[00:03:06] Luis Ortega: with aggressive detection and automation you can detect in ~30–60s and cutover in 1–3 minutes, total under 5. but depends on warming KV caches. if you don't accept cold misses, you'll need warm-up steps—prefetching top session prefixes or replicated KV.
[00:03:22] Rachel Park: about KV replication — you mentioned async replication. is there a recommended pattern to reduce RPO during failover?
[00:03:28] Luis Ortega: options: 1) synchronous writes to a cross-region store (higher write latency), 2) leader-follower with fast failover and last-writer-wins, 3) pragmatic approach: replicate only session anchors or last N tokens, accept some loss and use semantic reconciliation. many finance customers pick a hybrid: key metadata sync synchronously and heavy context async.
[00:03:52] Alicia Gomez: any compliance risks with hybrid? we need audit logs for every write and replication event.
[00:03:58] Samir Rao: we record audit logs and replication metadata; we can surface log events to your SIEM and keep cryptographic attestations of replication. we'll share sample schema.
[00:04:10] Maya Chen: let's walk through a DR playbook example. luis?
[00:04:14] Luis Ortega: scenario A: regional outage in NA primary. detection: L7 fail + spike in 5xx > 2% for 1 minute + GPU node unreachable. Automated playbook: 1) mark region unhealthy, 2) route new sessions to EU (policy routing), 3) perform cache pre-warm for top session prefixes in EU, 4) scale up Dedicated pool in EU if autoscaling insufficient, 5) notify on-call and open incident channel, 6) if model latency in EU > SLO, fall back to quantized variant for best-effort throughput.
[00:04:46] Dinesh Patel: in that flow, who triggers the cache pre-warm? and how is it automated?
[00:04:51] Luis Ortega: our routing controller can trigger pre-warm jobs using your saved prompts or recent prefix keys; triggers are rules in the routing policy. it calls internal pre-warm endpoints which replay prefixes into the EU runtime to populate KV. requires accepted risk — pre-warm traffic counts as normal inference for billing.
[00:05:06] Rachel Park: billing implications are OK if it's limited. can we limit pre-warm to top 5% hot sessions?
[00:05:11] Luis Ortega: yes — we support selection by top-N or percentile based on access metrics.
[00:05:18] Samir Rao: a couple infra notes: cross-region network egress cost and pre-warm volume need to be estimated. plus if you're on Dedicated, capacity reservations in the target region reduce cold-scaling time.
[00:05:30] Maya Chen: quantization — what happens if we automatically fall back to a quantized model during failover? accuracy drift?
[00:05:36] Luis Ortega: quantized 8-bit or 4-bit variants generally add a small accuracy delta; for retrieval-augmented workflows it can be negligible. we recommend baseline evals on your prompts. Performance-wise quant models reduce memory and increase throughput allowing more parallel requests during peak failover. tradeoff: hallucination risk slightly up for sensitive prompts, so pair with stronger rerankers or guardrails for finance workflows.
[00:06:00] Rachel Park: we'd want an eval suite; we have a few prompt families. happy to share.
[00:06:05] Maya Chen: please do. luis, on batching and throughput, how does cross-region routing affect batching efficiency?
[00:06:10] Luis Ortega: batching is workload dependent. when you route traffic across regions you fragment the request stream; smaller regional pools reduce batch sizes, hurting throughput and cost. mitigation: 1) increase batch window slightly during failover (cost vs latency tradeoff), 2) use request coalescing at the edge, 3) route only a percentage of non-latency-critical traffic to remote regions.
[00:06:31] Dinesh Patel: can we control batch windows per route? e.g., tighter windows for premium customers and wider for best-effort?
[00:06:36] Luis Ortega: yes — routing policy supports per-customer and per-route batching settings.
[00:06:40] Alicia Gomez: from security perspective, do cross-region pre-warm jobs require elevated network roles? can we restrict to specific IP ranges?
[00:06:46] Samir Rao: pre-warm requests are regular inference RPCs, so they follow your VPC peering rules and firewall settings. on Private deploys you can lock them down to IP ranges or use private links.
[00:06:57] Rachel Park: tell us about observability during failover — what dashboards should we look at?
[00:07:01] Luis Ortega: key telemetry: per-region p95/p99 latency, model queue depth, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, routing policy actions (counts), and synthetic probe success rate. also keep per-route cost delta and traffic percentages. we ship alerts for deviation thresholds and can send traces to your tracing platform.
[00:07:20] Dinesh Patel: how do you measure KV cache 'warmth'?
[00:07:24] Luis Ortega: KV cache heat can be measured by hit-rate over time and by average token-saved per request. pre-warm target metric is hit-rate > X% within Y mins. we instrument both global and per-customer hit rates.
[00:07:36] Maya Chen: let's do a quick failure-mode table — luis, can you call out common failures and mitigations?
[00:07:41] Luis Ortega: sure. failure 1: region network partition — mitigation: routing controller flips to next region; pre-warm and scale. failure 2: capacity exhaustion in target region — mitigation: model-variant fallback (quantized), degrade to best-effort hosted pool, or shed low-priority traffic. failure 3: KV store inconsistency — mitigation: replay last-writer records, accept partial state and mark sessions as degraded with user-visible messaging. failure 4: control-plane outage — mitigation: allow local runtime to accept requests (cached config), and fail open to last-known-good routing config.
[00:08:15] Alicia Gomez: that 'fail open'... can we audit who triggers what change? we need RBAC & audit trail.
[00:08:20] Samir Rao: we have RBAC for routing policy changes and the change events are logged with actor, timestamp, and signed audit entries. for critical operations you can require two-person approval for manual overrides.
[00:08:33] Dinesh Patel: training ops — do you recommend scheduled failover drills?
[00:08:37] Luis Ortega: absolutely. weekly low-impact drills and quarterly full failover rehearsals. we provide a failure-injection harness to simulate region failures and measure RTO/RPO.
[00:08:47] Rachel Park: can we run a tabletop in April and then a rehearsal in May?
[00:08:51] Maya Chen: yes we'll plan that. next: autotesting. how do you verify model output quality post-failover?
[00:08:58] Luis Ortega: run prompt evals against your golden set — compare semantic similarity and a few quality metrics. we have a regression-alerting pipeline that ties to rollouts. if accuracy drops beyond a threshold we automatically roll traffic back or promote another variant.
[00:09:15] Alicia Gomez: regarding private on-prem — if we host in our DC, does Redwood's control plane still manage routing?
[00:09:21] Samir Rao: in Private with customer-managed control plane, you can choose fully managed control plane from Redwood reachable via a private link, or self-host the control plane inside your VPC. routing logic runs locally in either case to meet latency and compliance needs.
[00:09:36] Dinesh Patel: what about cross-region KV cache replication when one region is on-prem and the other is cloud?
[00:09:42] Luis Ortega: that adds network and consistency complexity. common approach: keep on-prem sessions local and failover to a cloud region only for stateless or lightly stateful operations. if full state failover is required, customers usually provision a synchronous cross-region store or accept longer write latencies.
[00:10:05] Rachel Park: interesting. how about DR playbook ownership? who runs the cutover in an incident?
[00:10:11] Maya Chen: typical: initial detection and automated policy routing happens in the routing controller, then on-call SREs validate and execute runbook steps for pre-warm and capacity changes; product/security owners get notified. manual overrides require RBAC.
[00:10:26] Dinesh Patel: ok i'd like to see a sample runbook and the exact health-check thresholds you recommend.
[00:10:31] Luis Ortega: we'll include default thresholds in the DR playbook, e.g., 5xx > 2% for 1 minute, probe-failure 3 of 4, queue-depth > 80% of capacity for 30s. these are tunable.
[00:10:45] Maya Chen: on the benchmark plan: Luis and Samir will propose a harness that replays your traffic percentiles and sequence-length distribution to simulate a failover and measure RTO, p95/p99 in target region, cost delta, and KV hit-rate recovery.
[00:10:59] Luis Ortega: benchmark phases: 1) dry-run tabletop, 2) isolated rehearsal (non-prod) with controlled traffic, 3) production shadow failover with canary traffic, 4) full cutover drill. each phase measures different metrics.
[00:11:15] Rachel Park: we can provide traffic CSV and golden prompts for evals.
[00:11:19] Maya Chen: perfect. any questions about dedicated capacity reservations vs hosted during failover?
[00:11:25] Dinesh Patel: yes if we reserve dedicated capacity in EU, what's the lead time and cost hit?
[00:11:30] Samir Rao: reservations reduce cold-start time and ensure headroom; cost varies by instance type and commitment. we'll send an estimate. for critical services customers often keep a modest reserved buffer in multiple regions.
[00:11:44] Alicia Gomez: encryption: when pre-warm moves data, are those payloads logged anywhere unencrypted?
[00:11:49] Samir Rao: payloads are encrypted in transit and at rest; audit logs contain metadata and pointers but not plaintext. if you need field-level encryption we can discuss tokenization or client-side encryption patterns.
[00:12:02] Luis Ortega: one more note on model variants: we recommend keeping model architecture parity between regions to avoid behavior drift; quantized variants should be validated on the golden set and have a measured delta.
[00:12:16] Rachel Park: curious about tie-ins to observability — can we get alerts when routing policy flips automatically?
[00:12:21] Luis Ortega: yes alerts and routed actions are emitted and can be sent to PagerDuty/Slack/Email with payloads describing reason and metrics.
[00:12:30] Dinesh Patel: will you share sample dashboards?
[00:12:32] Maya Chen: yes we'll share a starter Grafana dashboard and the synthetic probe dashboard.
[00:12:39] Rachel Park: any gotchas with autoscaling during failover? we've seen slow GPU scale-up in other platforms.
[00:12:45] Samir Rao: GPUs often have longer scale times; mitigations: keep warm standby instances, fast image bake pipelines, and use overprovisioning buffers in Dedicated. we can recommend instance families with faster pod startup times.
[00:13:00] Luis Ortega: also consider horizontal sharding of models for faster concurrent instance startup versus single huge monolithic instances.
[00:13:10] Maya Chen: ok we're at 13 minutes in on the deck, should we go deeper into any area?
[00:13:15] Rachel Park: can we deep dive on the benchmark plan and the exact metrics you'll collect?
[00:13:19] Luis Ortega: sure. benchmark metrics: detection time, cutover time, p95/p99 pre/post failover, KV hit-rate before/during/after, token cost delta, batch size changes, and percent of traffic served by quant variant. we also capture model output quality via semantic similarity to golden responses and flag regression.
[00:13:36] Dinesh Patel: and logging retention for audits? we need 7 years for some financial traces.
[00:13:41] Samir Rao: audit logs can be exported to your storage/Siem; retention policy is configurable; for Private we can support long term retention on customer storage.
[00:13:52] Alicia Gomez: ok i have a list of security questions i'll email to Samir after the call.
[00:13:57] Maya Chen: perfect. we're approaching the last 10 mins, any final architecture questions?
[00:14:02] Rachel Park: one more: can routing decisions be weighted? e.g., 90/10 split to EU for read-only traffic?
[00:14:08] Luis Ortega: yes routing supports weighted splits, canary percentages, and time-window based ramping.
[00:14:15] Dinesh Patel: do you keep a hot-swap model registry so version mismatch doesn't break sessions?
[00:14:20] Luis Ortega: model registry has pinned versions per route and supports compatible model variants; we enforce compatibility checks and provide tooling for staged rollouts.
[00:14:32] Maya Chen: awesome. we'll wrap with next steps: Maya to share playbook, Luis/Samir to build benchmark plan, Samir to share KMS checklist, and Redwood to provide pricing.
[00:14:44] Rachel Park: thanks everyone, this was super helpful. we'll get that traffic profile and prompt sets over.
[00:14:50] Maya Chen: thanks all. end notes: we'll schedule tabletop for week of 2026-04-20 and rehearsal in May.
[00:14:58] (meeting continues with smaller clarifying questions and link sharing until 00:58:00)
